**Dynamics** are the volume of the music: how loud or quiet it is, and how that changes.

## 1. The markings

Dynamics are written as Italian words, shortened to letters.

| Marking | Italian | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| ***pp*** | pianissimo | very quiet |
| ***p*** | piano | quiet |
| ***mp*** | mezzo piano | moderately quiet |
| ***mf*** | mezzo forte | moderately loud |
| ***f*** | forte | loud |
| ***ff*** | fortissimo | very loud |
| **cresc.** or a widening hairpin `<` | crescendo | getting gradually louder |
| **dim.** / **decresc.** or a closing hairpin `>` | diminuendo / decrescendo | getting gradually quieter |
| ***sfz*** or ***sf*** | sforzando | a sudden strong accent on one note |

*Piano* is the Italian for quiet; the instrument's full name, *pianoforte*, means "quiet-loud", because it could play both.

The same phrase at three levels:

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:p, then mf, then ff
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:F
!p!F A c A|F4|!mf!F A c A|F4|!ff!F A c A|F4|]
</script></div>

## 2. Crescendo and diminuendo

A **hairpin** opens as the music gets louder and closes as it gets quieter. Always say where it starts *and* where it
ends up: a crescendo from ***p*** to ***f*** is a different thing from one from ***mf*** to ***ff***.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="96"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Crescendo from pp to ff, then a diminuendo back down
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
!pp!!crescendo(!C D E F|G A B !crescendo)!!ff!c|!diminuendo(!c B A G|F E D !diminuendo)!!pp!C|]
</script></div>

A **sforzando** hits one note hard and drops back at once:

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:p, with a sforzando on the third beat of each measure
M:3/4
L:1/4
K:Dm
!p!D F !sfz!A|D F !sfz!A|D F !sfz!A|D3|]
</script></div>

## 3. Where they go on the score

- For an instrument on one [staff]{.nn}: **under** the [staff]{.nn}.
- For piano: **between the two staves**, so one marking covers both hands.
- For voices: **above** the [staff]{.nn}, so the dynamics don't get mixed up with the words underneath.

## 4. Dynamics through history

| Period | Dynamics |
|---|---|
| **Baroque** (about 1600–1750) | few markings, mostly ***p*** and ***f***; **terraced dynamics**: sudden steps between loud and quiet sections (often by more or fewer instruments playing), not gradual changes |
| **Classical** (about 1750–1820) | more markings, crescendos and diminuendos, used for contrast; the new piano could play both quiet and loud |
| **Romantic** (about 1800–1910) | a huge range, from ***ppp*** to ***fff***, with constant crescendos and diminuendos for expression |

Terraced against gradual:

::: {.ax-pair}
<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="110" data-sound="harpsichord"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Terraced: a loud phrase, then its quiet echo
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:D
!f!d2 fd A2 dA|F2 AF D4|!p!d2 fd A2 dA|F2 AF D4|]
</script></div>

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="110"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Gradual: the same notes, one long crescendo
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:D
!p!!crescendo(!d2 fd A2 dA|F2 AF D4|d2 fd A2 dA|F2 AF !crescendo)!!f!D4|]
</script></div>
:::

## 5. Describing what you hear

When you describe dynamics in a listening question, **describe the changes in order**. One word for the whole piece is not
enough unless it really never changes.

> The music starts ***p***... then a gradual crescendo to ***f*** when the brass come in... a sudden drop to ***pp*** for
> the quiet middle section... then it ends ***ff***.

Useful words: *sudden*, *gradual*, *a wide range*, *a narrow range*, *contrast*, *terraced*, *fades out*.

## 6. Writing your own

- Give every entry a starting dynamic.
- A crescendo needs somewhere to go: mark where it ends.
- Contrast is what the ear notices. A piece that is ***mf*** throughout sounds flat, however good the notes.
